cells.tense: You are at the bench now, and the work is deepening under your hands.
cells.ask: Take one ordinary piece of what you are building and give it one more careful pass today, slower than the last. Then set it down.
cells.core:
Nothing is forcing this. You sit down with the work and it answers — an edge you can feel getting truer, a habit that pays a little more each time you come back to it. That is the whole strangeness: the deepening feels like patient attention, and it is happening now, under your hands, while most things in this stretch of life are still unsettled.

Being this early in something usually means scattered starts. Yours runs the other way — the craft itself is what keeps you in place. Give one piece of the work your full attention for a few minutes and then leave it alone. Care before force is what keeps this shape.

cells.verb: Deepening by dedicated craft, each pass cut a little nearer the mark

cells.tense: You are already living past this part, at a finish line that has not been reached yet.
cells.ask: Before you touch the work today, tell one person what you are trying to get good at, and leave it there. No progress report.
cells.core:
You keep treating what is still open as something to close, fast. Somewhere ahead is the version where this is finished, mastered, proof — and you are straining toward it before the thing you are building has told you what it is. The hurry is not building the skill. It is turning the work into a test you can lose, and the pressure is eating the pleasure that got you here.

What is already true: this takes years, not weekends. There is no clock except the one you carried in. Let somebody else hear the goal, once, plainly, with nothing to report yet. Saying it out loud is what lets the work stay a craft instead of a measure of you.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the door of something you already walked through.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are good at and say plainly what you can do now that you could not do a year ago. Out loud, to someone.
cells.core:
You did the early passes — the clumsy first versions, the ones that did not work — and you talk about all of it as if it were still the beginning. It isn't. Something quietly accumulated while you were busy being unsure, and you have been treating your own skill like a rumor you are not entitled to confirm.

That is why the work keeps feeling like a question: the claim was never put in the room. Name what you can do now that you could not do before, once, out loud, without qualifying it. The craft moves forward when you stand behind what it has already made of you.
cells.sheetLine: You learned something somewhere and still call it the beginning.

cells.tense: You are building toward mastery while telling yourself it is only a hobby.
cells.ask: Write down what you actually want out of this practice, one sentence, as yours. Not what it is for. What you want.
cells.core:
You have been at this long enough that the first crude versions are gone and the passes are getting finer. But when anyone asks, you shrug — a hobby, a way to pass an evening, nothing serious — even as it takes your best attention. The dedication is real and it is running. The saying-so is what is missing.

Wanting something from your own practice is not greed. If this is heading somewhere, say where you would like it to go, in your own words, and let that be true while the thing is still unfinished. Direction and momentum move best together here; they only cannot while one of them is denied.
